outputs.L3:
# The Elemental Center

The elemental center of existence has always been present, cycling eternally like the seasons and their recorded rhythms. Long before human hands began marking calendars or setting down observations in ledgers, the earth turned through its seasons with the same patient constancy it maintains today. Spring followed winter, summer followed spring, and autumn came to gather what had grown—an unbroken procession that predates memory itself and will outlast every observer who has ever paused to notice it.

This ancient rhythm finds its human counterpart in a deep love of order, reflected in the careful documentation of nature that country people have practiced for generations. The recording of swallow migrations—their arrival dates noted year after year in the same hand, on the same page—speaks to something beyond mere curiosity. So too does the counting of grouse across the moorland, or the careful tallying of stocked fish quotas in rivers and lakes. These are not idle exercises but a form of devotion, a way of participating in the natural order by bearing witness to it, of imposing a small, comprehensible structure upon the vast unknowability of the wild.

The high sheep country and hill-farms offer a particular kind of relief from politics, from the noise and contention of the wider world. Here, walking among the folds and drystone walls, one can feel restored to an ancient connection to the land—one that predates nations and their quarrels. This connection lives on in the dialect names for skies and clouds, words passed down through generations of shepherds and farmers who needed no meteorologist to tell them what the heavens portended. These names carry within them centuries of observation, a vernacular science as precise in its own way as any modern forecast, yet steeped in local character and inherited wisdom.

Within this world exists a simple, quiet domestic life: dreaming, pottering about the house, listening to local radio as the day unfolds. There is something transformative in this apparent ordinariness. The mundane news of the parish—a death, a wedding, the price of lambs at market—takes on, in this context, a profound sense of pure existence. It is not that these small events are dramatic in themselves, but that they occur within a rhythm so old and so deeply felt that even the trivial becomes charged with significance, each broadcast a small affirmation that life continues in its accustomed way.

In this remote, elevated part of Ireland, the landscape holds a unique stillness and an ambivalent light—neither wholly bright nor wholly shadowed, but suspended in some quality peculiar to high, isolated places. It is a light that seems to hold time itself in abeyance. Even historical menace, evoked by figures as disparate as Vladimir and Estragon waiting beside their tree, or the shadowy passage of commandos and insurgents through such terrain in darker decades, loses its power to frighten here. The mountain absorbs these ghosts of violence and absurdity alike, folding them into its greater stillness, until what remains is not fear but a kind of peace—the sense that whatever human drama has passed through this place, the land itself persists, indifferent and enduring, cycling always back to its own elemental center.
outputs.L4:
# In the Hill Country

Here, in this fold between two mountains,
the year turns like a wheel that has forgotten
it was ever meant to arrive anywhere.
The turf is cut in June, stacked by August,
burned through winters that repeat themselves
so faithfully the old men no longer bother
naming which year brought the hardest frost.

Below the pass, the sheep move without urgency
from summer grass to winter shelter, back again,
tracing paths worn deep by grandfathers
who are, in some sense, still walking them—
their boots long gone to dust, their knowledge
passed down not in words but in the way
a hand still knows to test the wind before opening a gate.

There is no news here that matters more
than whether rain will come before the hay is in,
no border that concerns the bog,
no parliament that governs when the blackthorn blooms.
The wireless mutters of the world below,
of votes and borders, marches, treaties signed—
but up here, meaning moves at the pace of moss,
and no one hurries to translate it.

I think sometimes of two men by a tree,
waiting for something that will not arrive,
filling the empty hours with talk of boots,
of turnips, of a rope that might or might not hold—
Vladimir and Estragon, patient in their absurdity,
and how this landscape, too, seems caught
in that same suspended patience, that same
willingness to wait without despair,
to let each day be merely what it is:
a stretch of pure existence, unadorned,
needing no more meaning than the light demands.

And the light here is ambivalent—
neither the gold of promise nor the grey of loss,
but something in between, hanging low
over turf smoke and wet stone walls,
uncertain whether to reveal or to conceal,
content instead to simply linger,
the way the mist lingers on the higher slopes
long after the valley below has woken.

Nowhere else, I think, does time behave this way—
not quite moving, not quite still,
but circling like the buzzard overhead,
riding some current invisible to us,
waiting, as we wait, for nothing
that requires a name.
outputs.L5:
# All, Eternally, Like

There is a thread that runs through all things—through mountains worn smooth by patient rivers, through the quiet breath of a sleeping child, through the vast dark spaces between stars. This thread does not discriminate; it touches the humble and the magnificent with equal tenderness.

We often search for what makes us different from one another, cataloging our distinctions like treasures. Yet perhaps the deeper truth lies in recognizing how alike we truly are. The grief of a stranger mirrors our own sorrow. The joy in a child's laughter echoes something universal, something we all recognize instantly, without translation.

To love eternally is not to escape time, but to plant something within it that outlasts the moment of its planting. A grandmother's recipe, passed down through generations. A kindness shown to someone who never forgets it. A truth spoken once that changes the course of a life. These things ripple outward, refusing to be contained by the boundaries of a single lifetime.

Perhaps this is the quiet miracle hidden in ordinary existence: that all of us, in our brief and flickering moments, participate in something that continues. We are like waves that rise and fall, yet the ocean itself remains, eternally reshaping itself while never truly disappearing.

So when we look at another person and feel that spark of recognition—that sense of *I understand you, I have felt what you feel*—we are touching something ancient and unbroken. All of us, in our separate stories, are somehow telling the same story. Like echoes in a canyon, our voices multiply, transform, and return to us in forms we could never have predicted, yet somehow always knew.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about the timeless rhythms of rural Irish life, weaving in a reference to Vladimir and Estragon from Waiting for Godot.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Long Acre

The bog holds its breath all winter,
black water remembering every foot
that ever crossed it, every cart wheel,
every coffin carried shoulder-high
to the small church on the hill.

Here, time moves like a cow through a gate—
unhurried, certain, chewing the cud
of another grey morning.
The men still stand at the crossroads
the way they always have,
caps pulled low, hands in pockets,
watching the road for something
that may or may not come.

They could be Vladimir and Estragon,
these two by the gate, this bare tree
that never quite decides to bloom—
*Nothing to be done*, one says,
and spits, and means it kindly,
the way you'd bless a stranger.
They have been waiting so long
they've forgotten what for—
the creamery lorry, the rain to lift,
some word from a son in England,
or only the evening itself,
which comes anyway, unbidden,
the way it always has.

The kettle sings its same thin song.
The dog turns three times before lying down.
The turf stack shrinks by winter
and grows again by autumn,
and somewhere a woman is churning
the same butter her mother churned,
her arm remembering the motion
before her mind does.

Godot doesn't come here either.
But the bread rises.
The cows come home unherded,
udders heavy, hooves finding
the same worn path through the fields,
and someone always opens the gate,
and someone always waits for someone
who is already home,
sitting by the fire,
waiting too.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemplative poem set in the Irish hill-country, exploring themes of order, seasonal repetition, and the "high right hand of Ireland."
counterfactuals.output:
**The High Right Hand**

Here in the hill-country the walls go up
in courses no plumb-line ever kept true,
stone laid on stone by hands long turned to dust,
and still they hold — a grammar of grey rock
declining through the bracken, sentence
after sentence, field to field, until
the whole hillside reads like a psalm half-learned,
repeated till the meaning wears to sound.

I have walked this ridge in every season
and found the same door always slightly open:
the whin in flower when nothing else will bloom,
the curlew's cry unspooling over bog
as it unspooled, they say, before the Flood,
the lambs come stumbling into cold Aprils
exactly as their mothers stumbled once,
the turf stacked black against November,
a ritual of hands that do not ask
why order matters, only that it does.

And over all of this, the long ridge lifts
its shoulder to the west — call it a hand,
the high right hand of Ireland, raised
not in command but in the shape of blessing,
the way a bishop's hand forgets itself
and simply opens, weather passing through it,
rain and sun alike let fall like coins
onto the fields below, indifferent, kind.

I do not know what governs — if the walls
were built to mirror something in the hills,
or if the hills themselves first taught the hands
their patient stubborn language of enclosure.
But every spring the same light finds the same
gap in the same wall, and falls there golden,
and something in me kneels to that repeating,
not from belief exactly, but from love
of pattern, the way water loves its channel,
the way the hand, grown old, still knows its work
and keeps on lifting, season after season,
against the sky that keeps on being there.

So let the ridge stand raised above the glen
in its slow gesture, half-forgotten blessing,
and let the walls keep saying what they say
in broken grammar to the passing cloud —
that order is a kind of prayer worn smooth,
that repetition is not weariness
but faithfulness, the shape that love takes on
when it has no more need of being new.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a literary poem in the style of Derek Mahon, focusing on rural stillness, weather fronts, and pastoral imagery like herons and sheep country.
counterfactuals.output:
**Weather Front, Sheep Country**

The whole glen holds its breath before the rain
comes walking in from Erris on grey feet.
Sheep gather like loose stones along the boreen,
their bells gone dumb, a stillness at the throat

of afternoon. Far off, the mountain wears
a cap of cloud it did not have an hour ago,
and something in the light — a coppery stain —
tells you the front is real, and coming slow.

A heron stands stock-still among the reeds,
one leg drawn up, a grey and folded thought
too patient for the world's impatient needs,
reading the water like a page half-caught

between two languages it half forgets.
He was here, they say, before the house was built,
before the field was field, before the gates
went up to keep the bog from what was tilled —

and will be here, no doubt, when we are gone,
when this whole valley's turned to something else,
some other use, some other name put on
the townland, and the turf-smoke's smell itself

a memory of a memory. For now
the rain arrives, soft-footed, gray and mild,
and settles on the wool of every ewe
like something we forgot we'd reconciled

ourselves to long ago — the slow, sure drift
of weather over sheep-cropped hill and stone,
indifferent, patient, neither loss nor gift,
just rain, just distance, coming down alone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a reflective, image-rich poem about escaping politics through nature—mentioning local radio, hill-farms, and the quiet vigilance of waiting, echoing Beckett's absurdist themes.
counterfactuals.output:
**Static and Pasture**

Turn the dial past the shouting men—
their voices thin as wire, snapping
against each other over borders,
budgets, the usual apocalypse—
until you find the local station,
a woman reading livestock prices
like a rosary: *lambs steady,
wool holding, rain expected
Thursday, maybe.*

Nothing to be done, the wind says,
combing through the gorse
with the patience of a saint
who's given up on saints.

Up here the hill-farms lean
into their own weather, stone walls
built by hands long since
folded into the ground they cleared.
A dog waits by a gate that hasn't
opened in an hour. He does not
question the gate. He has made
a philosophy of waiting,
the way the sheep have made
a religion of grass—
each day the same sermon,
each day somehow enough.

I have come here to unlearn
the news, its need to name
every silence a crisis.
The radio crackles, loses signal
in the dip between two hills
and I let it go, let the static
become its own kind of psalm—
snow-hiss, empty church,
a held breath that never
quite finishes exhaling.

Estragon and Vladimir would understand
this bench, this view, this waiting
for a bus that may not come
because the road itself
seems to have reconsidered.
Nothing arrives. Everything is arriving.
The fence posts count the field
like a rosary of their own devising,
believing in nothing
but the next post,
and the next,

and still the farmer walks his rounds
each dusk, as if the walking
were the point, as if tomorrow
required this exact rehearsal—
boots, gate, dog, the same
five words to the sheep
who've heard them
ten thousand times
and listen anyway,

the way I listen now
to nothing, to wind,
to a radio signal thinning
to a single trembling wire
that might be a voice,
might be the shape a voice
leaves behind—

and either way, I wait.
Either way, the hills keep their weather.
Either way, someone somewhere
is boiling water for tea
that will grow cold before
the answer comes,
if the answer
was ever coming,

if there was ever
a question at all
beyond this: the grass,
the gate, the going on.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a meditative poem on permanence and light in the Irish countryside, incorporating both natural details (swallows, grouse, rainbows) and an allusion to a famous existentialist play.
counterfactuals.output:
# Waiting for the Light at Ballyvaughan

Here the stone walls hold what water cannot—
a permanence of grey, arranged by hands
long gone to dust, still standing though the boot
of every century has walked these lands.

The swallows come regardless of our watch,
stitch summer to the eaves with threads of flight,
and disappear again before we catch
the meaning that they carve against the light.

A rainbow bridges Corrib to the sea,
one moment's arch that no one can possess—
we stand beneath its brief geometry
as if the color proves our permanence.

Somewhere a grouse breaks cover, low and sure,
its wingbeat like a door that shuts on time.
We wait here too, the way we've waited for
some Godot in the hawthorn and the lime—

not knowing if he's late or never was,
not knowing if the waiting is the thing,
while light moves slow across the rush and gorse
the way it moved before, and now, this spring.

The bog holds bodies older than the church,
the church holds prayers older than the state,
and we hold nothing but this present search
for reasons we keep watching, keep this wait

beside the wall that will outlast our watching,
under a sky that empties and refills,
where nothing stays except the light's slow touching
of things that pass—the swallows, and the hills.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
